one_liner: Educational C++20 fixed-size pool and first-fit free-list allocators; the pool beats macOS malloc/free on bulk 16 B allocation.
what_it_does: Two single-threaded allocators with their own interfaces, not a malloc replacement. mem::PoolAllocator(blockSize, blockCount, alignment) hands out fixed-size slots from one pre-allocated chunk through Allocate()/Free()/Reset(). mem::FreeListAllocator(totalBytes, FitPolicy) serves variable sizes and alignments from one pre-reserved arena, splitting blocks on allocation and coalescing them on free.
how_it_is_fast: The pool is a classic intrusive free list (a slab allocator): each free slot's first 8 bytes point to the next free slot, so Allocate and Free are a single pointer pop or push with no size classes, locking or metadata lookup. The free-list allocator is textbook first-fit (or best-fit) over a doubly linked free list, with boundary headers holding physical prev/next links for coalescing. It walks the list linearly, so it is not a fast path.
when_to_use: Single-threaded code that allocates many same-sized objects (nodes, particles, entities) and knows an upper bound on their count up front
Frame-style workloads that can drop everything at once with PoolAllocator::Reset()
As a small, readable reference for how slab and free-list allocators work before adopting a production allocator
Vendoring about 300 lines of MIT code when a full allocator dependency is not wanted
when_not_to_use: Any multithreaded allocation: neither allocator is thread-safe and there are no thread caches
As a general malloc replacement: FreeListAllocator was slower than macOS malloc in its own sample (8.06 ms vs 5.68 ms bulk at 16 B) and does a linear first-fit search
When the object count is unbounded: the pool returns nullptr once exhausted and never grows
Security-sensitive code: no guard pages, no poisoning, no ownership check in PoolAllocator::Free
Production use in general: one commit, 1 star, and the author calls it an educational/portfolio implementation

integration.platforms: any (build instructions are macOS-only; no platform-specific code seen)
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe; the README says to wrap it in a mutex
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: a separate class API (Allocate/Free on an allocator object), no malloc/operator new override and no std::allocator adapter

gotchas: The README says both allocators assert on double free, but only FreeListAllocator::Free has that assert; PoolAllocator::Free has no double-free or ownership check and silently corrupts the free list.

PoolAllocator rounds blockSize up only to sizeof(void*), not to the requested alignment, so a block size that is not a multiple of the alignment (e.g. 24 B with 16 B alignment) returns misaligned slots after the first one. The benchmark sizes are all multiples of 16, so they are unaffected.

Harness bias: the pool's constructor, outside the timed region, threads the free list through every slot and so pre-faults all pages, while the malloc bulk timing includes first-touch page faults. The churn column shows malloc at 0.00 ms, which is consistent with the compiler eliding the unused malloc/free pair, so churn comparisons are meaningless.

blockSize * blockCount is not checked for overflow, and FreeListAllocator stores an 8-byte offset before every user pointer plus a 48-byte header, so per-allocation overhead is large for 16 B objects.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only for learning, or to vendor a minimal single-threaded pool; NotKeira/fast-alloc gives a similar pool with Linux numbers on a named CPU, and Bloodmoon001/memory-allocator and privateMwb/ArenaAllocator cover the same educational niche. For anything general-purpose, use the catalogued malloc replacements (mimalloc-class allocators, IsoAlloc, Mesh).
verified_claims_summary: The README's sample output, measured on an unspecified macOS machine (Apple clang, -O2, Release), shows the pool completing 200000 16-byte allocations and frees in bulk in 0.89 ms against 5.68 ms for macOS malloc/free (about 6.4x, derived from page data). The free-list allocator was slower (8.06 ms), and the churn column is not usable because malloc reads 0.00 ms. The README's '5-15x' and 'FreeList clearly faster on churn' claims are not supported by its own sample.
status_note: One initial commit (2026-09-23) on a 1-star MIT repo labelled educational by its author; small enough to read and vendor, but not hardened.
